decision: Use a numerical polynomial growth exponent with absolute error at most 1/100, replacing the earlier constant-factor asymptotic target.
general_rule: A numerical target, including a defined complexity exponent, uses absolute 1/100 accuracy unless an explicit exact-answer exception applies.
source_scope: Original equal-length binary-word question and logarithmic-state endpoint; no new current-status review.

before.formal: Determine, up to constant factors as \(n\to\infty\), \[s(n)=\max_{\substack{u,v\in\{0,1\}^n\\u\ne v}}\min\{|Q|:\text{a DFA with state set }Q\text{ accepts exactly one of }u,v\}.\]
before.definitions: The parameter \(n\) is a positive integer and both words have exactly \(n\) symbols. A deterministic finite automaton (DFA) consists of a finite nonempty set \(Q\), one initial state \(q_0\), a total transition function \(\delta:Q\times\{0,1\}\to Q\), and an accepting set \(F\subseteq Q\). It reads its word once from left to right, starting at \(q_0\), applies \(\delta\) for each symbol and accepts exactly when its final state lies in \(F\). There are no epsilon transitions, auxiliary storage or external position counters. All states, including any rejecting sink, count toward size. The automaton may depend on the pair of words, and either orientation of acceptance is allowed. Its behavior on other words is unrestricted. The minimum is finite, since a DFA can recognize a singleton word, and the maximum is over a finite nonempty set of pairs. No efficiency requirement is imposed on finding the automaton. A proposed positive comparison function \(f\) determines the requested asymptotic scale when constants \(a,b>0\) and \(n_0\) exist with \(a f(n)\le s(n)\le b f(n)\) for every integer \(n\ge n_0\). The source’s conjectured endpoint is \(s(n)=O(\log n)\); the card explicitly asks for the underlying worst-case scale rather than asserting this endpoint.
before.answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous positive comparison function \(f(n)\) and a Lean proof of both constant-factor inequalities in the definitions. A universal small-DFA upper bound must be accompanied by a matching worst-case lower bound. This is asymptotic state complexity; the numerical 0.01 tolerance does not apply to big-O bounds. Results for random words or selected families of pairs do not determine the unrestricted maximum.

sentences: The problem measures the smallest deterministic automaton that distinguishes two binary words of equal length.
A different automaton may be chosen for each pair and its behavior on other words is unrestricted.
The target is the worst-case number of states as a function of the common word length.
The original question proposes a logarithmic upper bound, while recent general bounds have a one-third power with logarithmic factors.
The benchmark asks for matching constant-factor asymptotics across all pairs, not a random-input guarantee.

context_blocks.text: The original problem asks whether logarithmically many states always suffice to distinguish two equal-length binary words. This card develops that threshold question into determination of the worst-case state function.

The August 2026 primary abstract reports a general \(\widetilde O(n^{1/3})\) upper bound and studies a stronger result only when one word is random. The September preprint supplies another proof at the general one-third exponent, not a logarithmic universal bound.

before.why: Determining this scale would quantify how little finite-state memory suffices to distinguish an arbitrary pair of long binary strings.

after.formal:
For each integer \(n\ge1\), let \(s(n)\) be the largest, over pairs of distinct binary words of length \(n\), minimum number of states in a deterministic finite automaton (DFA) that accepts exactly one of the two words. The automaton model is specified in Definitions and model below.

Determine the polynomial growth exponent
\[
x_* = \inf\bigl\{r\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}:s(n)=O(n^r)\bigr\}
\]
to absolute error at most \(1/100\). The asymptotic bound inside this definition is quantified explicitly below; the target is the exponent, rather than the entire function up to constant factors.
after.definitions:
The parameter \(n\) is a positive integer and both words have exactly \(n\) symbols. A deterministic finite automaton (DFA) consists of a finite nonempty set \(Q\), one initial state \(q_0\), a total transition function \(\delta:Q\times\{0,1\}\to Q\), and an accepting set \(F\subseteq Q\). It reads its word once from left to right, starting at \(q_0\), applies \(\delta\) for each symbol and accepts exactly when its final state lies in \(F\). There are no epsilon transitions, auxiliary storage or external position counters. All states, including any rejecting sink, count toward size. The automaton may depend on the pair of words, and either orientation of acceptance is allowed. Its behavior on other words is unrestricted. The minimum is finite, since a DFA can recognize a singleton word, and the maximum is over a finite nonempty set of pairs. No efficiency requirement is imposed on finding the automaton.

Precisely, write
\[
s(n)=\max_{\substack{u,v\in\{0,1\}^n\\u\ne v}}
\min\bigl\{|Q|:\text{a DFA with state set }Q\text{ accepts exactly one of }u,v\bigr\}.
\]
The maximum and minimum use the model above. A complete DFA recognizing one fixed length-\(n\) word has at most \(n+2\) states, so \(1\le s(n)\le n+2\).

The polynomial growth exponent is the infimum (greatest lower bound)
\[
x_* = \inf\left\{r\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}:\ \exists C>0\ \exists N\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\ \forall n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge N},\quad s(n)\le Cn^r\right\}.
\]
The constants \(C,N\) may depend on \(r\), but not on \(n\) or the pair of words. The defining set is nonempty and bounded below, and \(0\le x_*\le1\). Its infimum need not belong to the set. Equivalently, \(x_*\) is the limit superior, or limiting upper envelope, of \(\log s(n)/\log n\) over integers \(n\ge2\); no existence of an ordinary limit is assumed.

For every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), the definition implies \(s(n)=O(n^{x_*+\varepsilon})\). It does not assume the stronger two-sided relation \(s(n)=n^{x_*+o(1)}\). A lower bound on the exponent may be established by worst-case pairs at arbitrarily large lengths; a guarantee on random words does not replace the worst-case definition of \(s(n)\).

The source's logarithmic endpoint \(s(n)=O(\log n)\) would imply \(x_*=0\), but the converse need not hold. Exponent zero also allows growth faster than every power of \(\log n\) but slower than every positive power of \(n\). The benchmark's additive tolerance applies to \(x_*\), not to the state count \(s(n)\).
after.answer_criterion:
Supply an unambiguously specified real number \(a\) and a complete Lean-checked proof that
\[
|a-x_*|\le1/100.
\]
An explicitly specified interval \([L,U]\) with \(U-L\le1/50\), together with a Lean proof that \(L\le x_*\le U\), qualifies via its midpoint. Exact determination also qualifies. The defining infimum alone, restated without locating its value, is not an answer.

The proof must certify both sides of the required interval for the exponent defined above. A universal automaton upper bound qualifies only when combined with a proved lower bound that gives the required numerical accuracy. The lower bound may use hard pairs at arbitrarily large lengths. There is no requirement to determine logarithmic factors, a leading constant, constant-factor asymptotics of \(s(n)\), or an automaton construction attaining the infimum. An answer within tolerance does not by itself prove the original logarithmic-state conjecture.

sentences: The problem asks how many states a deterministic finite automaton needs to distinguish two binary words of the same length.
For each length, take the hardest pair after choosing the smallest separating automaton separately for each pair.
The numerical target is the infimum exponent for which that worst-case state count has a polynomial upper bound.
A benchmark answer must locate this exponent within absolute error 0.01 with a Lean-checked proof.
Determining the exponent does not require matching logarithmic factors or proving the source’s stronger logarithmic-state conjecture.
